analysis.one_liner: Makes drug companies pay bigger Medicaid rebates and lower federal prices on drugs they advertise to consumers.
analysis.headline: The Senate referred the bill to the Finance Committee in May 2005 and it never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required drug manufacturers that run TV, radio, print, or billboard ads aimed at consumers to pay larger rebates to state Medicaid programs and to sell at lower negotiated prices to federal health programs, including the Department of Veterans Affairs, the Department of Defense, the Indian Health Service, and the 340B program for community clinics. Manufacturers that certified a drug was not advertised directly to consumers would have been exempt. It also would have required a report to Congress on how much advertising-driven drug spending is passed on to federal health programs.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicaid programs and their beneficiaries, veterans and military families who get care through the VA and Defense Health Program, patients of community clinics and the Indian Health Service, and taxpayers who fund these programs — all would have paid less for heavily advertised brand-name drugs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicaid and VA patients, and taxpayers

how_it_helps.text: Medicaid would receive an increased rebate for any covered outpatient drug a manufacturer advertised directly to consumers through TV, radio, print, or outdoor advertising, with the rebate formula adjusted to account for the added cost advertising pushes onto state programs.

Federal purchasers — the Public Health Service and Indian Health Service (including the 340B drug pricing program), the VA, and the Defense Department — would pay a negotiated reduced price for any drug whose manufacturer could not certify it was not consumer-advertised in the prior 12 months.

By January 2007, HHS would have had to report to Congress on how much of the cost of consumer-advertised drugs is passed to federal programs, the 25 most prescribed and 25 most costly such drugs, aggregate manufacturer advertising spending, and strategies to ensure federal drug purchases reflect health need rather than marketing.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers that advertise directly to consumers would bear higher rebates and lower federal purchase prices; the advertising industry would lose the incentive revenue from ads these companies might pull to avoid the penalty.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name drug makers and ad sellers

drawbacks.text: The bill left the size of the increased Medicaid rebate to a formula adjustment determined by the Secretary of Health and Human Services after consulting manufacturers, so the savings for state programs would depend on unelected officials' choices rather than being fixed in law.

The bill targeted only federal programs and Medicaid; Americans with private insurance or no coverage would have seen no direct price relief, since the mechanism works through government rebates and contracts.

Drug companies argued then, as now, that consumer advertising informs patients about treatable conditions; this bill addressed that argument by making advertising costly to the advertiser, which could have led manufacturers to pull ads rather than cut prices — a defensible outcome, but one that reduces public information as a side effect.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The mechanism is narrow but real: it taxes a specific behavior (consumer advertising) through bigger rebates and lower federal prices, so the savings fall where drug spending is heaviest and drug companies could avoid the penalty simply by not advertising. The main weakness is that it would not have lowered prices for people outside Medicaid and the named federal programs, and it delegated the rebate formula to administrative discretion.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate read the bill twice and sent it to the Finance Committee, where no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Sen. Ron Wyden introduced the bill on May 26, 2005, joined by Republican Sen. John Sununu as its sole cosponsor.
On the day it was introduced, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance.
The action history shows no further activity of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no committee report, and no floor vote — for the remainder of the 109th Congress, which ended January 3, 2007.

The bill would have raised Medicaid rebates for consumer-advertised drugs and required the Public Health Service (including the Indian Health Service and 340B program), the VA, and the Defense Department to pay reduced negotiated prices for drugs their makers could not certify as unadvertised.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers that advertise to consumers kept their existing Medicaid rebate terms and federal purchase prices untouched, because the bill never advanced past committee. The advertising industry kept the revenue stream as well.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumer-advertised drug makers and ad sellers

for.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate and gave introductory remarks on it.

for.name: Sen. John Sununu
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it a bipartisan two-senate effort.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance (Chair Chuck Grassley)
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over Medicaid and Medicare
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it died in committee at the end of the 109th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship — one Democrat and one Republican — but it was a Democratic-led effort in a Republican-controlled Senate that never reached the floor, so no roll-call shows how the parties would have split.

industries.note: Companies that advertise drugs directly to consumers would owe larger Medicaid rebates and accept reduced negotiated prices from the VA, Pentagon, Indian Health Service, and 340B clinics. Their interest in keeping ad-driven prices for these programs runs against the patients and taxpayers paying them.

Since the penalty attaches to consumer advertising on TV, radio, print, and outdoor media, drug makers facing higher rebates would have an incentive to cut those ads, shrinking a major prescription-drug advertising revenue stream.
